name: Indonesia
tagline: The world's largest archipelago, where volcanoes, rice terraces, coral reefs and Komodo dragons sit scattered across more than seventeen thousand islands.
cardDescription: Bali's temples and rice terraces, Java's volcanoes and ancient stupas, and the wild islands of Komodo and Raja Ampat further east.
metaDescription: A complete Indonesia travel guide: the 10 best places to visit, Bali, Borobudur, Komodo dragons, Raja Ampat diving, costs and a practical ten-day itinerary.

image.file: File:Padar Island, Komodo National Park, Indonesia, 20250822 0929 2659.jpg
image.alt: The dramatic multi-bay silhouette of Padar Island in Komodo National Park, Indonesia

intro: Indonesia is genuinely difficult to summarise, because it isn't really one place — it's more than seventeen thousand islands spread across three time zones, home to hundreds of distinct languages and cultures, from Hindu Bali to Islamic Java to the animist highlands of Sumatra and the wild eastern frontier of Papua.

Most visitors genuinely start with Bali, and it earns the attention — rice terraces, surf breaks, temples and a genuinely warm, ritual-rich culture — but Bali is a single small island in a country that also holds an active volcano you can watch erupt from a safe distance, a UNESCO temple complex bigger than most cathedrals, wild Komodo dragons, and reefs in Raja Ampat that marine biologists consider the richest on Earth.

The scale genuinely shapes how you should plan a trip: island-hopping here means real flights and ferries, not quick day trips, so most visitors pick two or three regions rather than trying to cover the whole archipelago in one go.
placesIntro: Ordered roughly by how strongly we would recommend each for a first visit — though Raja Ampat and Lake Toba reward a second trip just as much as a first.
thingsToDoIntro: The experiences that recur across the archipelago and that make an Indonesia trip feel like more than a Bali beach holiday.

thingsToDo.title: Watch the sunrise over an active volcano

image.file: File:View from Bromo mountain before sunrise, Java, Indonesia, 20220820 0510 9327.jpg
image.alt: Sunrise over Mount Bromo's volcanic crater in East Java

thingsToDo.text: Mount Bromo genuinely delivers one of Southeast Asia's great sunrise views, a smoking crater rising out of a sea of mist and volcanic sand.
thingsToDo.tip: Book a jeep the genuinely night before — the viewpoint car park fills fast in the pre-dawn dark.

thingsToDo.title: See wild Komodo dragons

image.alt: A wild Komodo dragon on Komodo Island, Indonesia

thingsToDo.text: Komodo and Rinca islands are genuinely the only places on Earth these giant monitor lizards still live wild, best seen with a ranger guide on a short walking trail.
thingsToDo.tip: Rinca genuinely offers a higher dragon-sighting chance than Komodo island itself, with a shorter, easier walk.

thingsToDo.title: Dive or snorkel a world-class reef

image.alt: Colourful coral reef and fish in Raja Ampat, Indonesia

thingsToDo.text: Raja Ampat genuinely holds the richest marine biodiversity recorded anywhere on Earth, though Komodo's reefs and Bali's Amed and Tulamben aren't far behind.
thingsToDo.tip: Raja Ampat's own best visibility window runs roughly October to April, genuinely opposite Bali and Komodo's dry season — check with operators before booking.

thingsToDo.title: Explore an ancient temple complex

image.alt: Borobudur temple at sunrise with a volcano visible in the background

thingsToDo.text: Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist temple, and nearby Hindu Prambanan are genuinely two of Southeast Asia's great ancient monuments, both UNESCO World Heritage sites.
thingsToDo.tip: A genuinely sunrise entry ticket at Borobudur gets you inside before the day-trip crowds arrive.

thingsToDo.title: Surf a world-class break

image.file: File:Uluwatu surf break landscape photo bali travel photos wokshots.jpg
image.alt: The surf break at Uluwatu, Bali, seen from the clifftop

thingsToDo.text: Bali's Bukit Peninsula genuinely holds some of the world's best-known breaks, from Uluwatu's barrels to Canggu's beginner-friendly beach breaks.
thingsToDo.tip: Dry season (April to October) genuinely brings the most consistent swell on Bali's south and west coasts.

thingsToDo.title: Relax on a car-free island

image.file: File:Gili Trawangan Island, Trees, Sunset, Indonesia.jpg
image.alt: Palm trees at sunset on Gili Trawangan island

thingsToDo.text: The Gili Islands off Lombok are genuinely car-free, with horse carts and bicycles the only transport and a laid-back pace to match.
thingsToDo.tip: Gili Trawangan is genuinely the liveliest of the three; Gili Meno is the quietest for an actual break.

foodIntro: Indonesian food's reputation abroad rarely does justice to a genuinely vast, regionally distinct cuisine spanning thousands of islands.

foods.name: Nasi goreng

image.alt: A plate of nasi goreng, Indonesian fried rice, topped with a fried egg

foods.text: Genuinely Indonesia's unofficial national dish, a smoky fried rice built around sweet soy sauce (kecap manis), usually topped with a fried egg.
foods.whereToTry: Warungs and restaurants nationwide, at every price point.

foods.name: Satay (sate)

image.alt: Skewers of Indonesian satay grilling over charcoal

foods.text: Genuinely ubiquitous grilled meat skewers, usually served with a rich peanut sauce, varying by region from Madura's chicken satay to Bali's minced lilit.
foods.whereToTry: Street carts and warungs nationwide, especially in the evening.

foods.name: Rendang

image.alt: A bowl of rendang, slow-cooked spiced beef from West Sumatra

foods.text: A genuinely slow-cooked Minangkabau beef dish from West Sumatra, simmered for hours in coconut milk and spices until deeply rich and dark.
foods.whereToTry: Padang restaurants nationwide, and especially in West Sumatra itself.

foods.name: Gado-gado

image.alt: A plate of gado-gado, an Indonesian vegetable salad with peanut sauce

foods.text: A genuinely satisfying vegetable and boiled-egg salad tossed in peanut sauce, one of Indonesia's most reliable options for vegetarians.
foods.whereToTry: Warungs nationwide, especially in Jakarta and Java.

foods.name: Nasi padang

image.alt: An array of nasi padang dishes served alongside rice

foods.text: A genuinely distinctive way of eating, with a dozen small dishes brought to your table at once and paid for only by what you actually take.
foods.whereToTry: Padang restaurants nationwide, identifiable by their stacked-dish window displays.

foods.name: Indonesian coffee (kopi)

image.file: File:Sangrai Biji Kopi secara traditional di Coffee Plantation Bali.jpg
image.alt: Traditional coffee roasting at a plantation in Bali

foods.text: Genuinely world-renowned coffee country, from Sumatra's earthy Mandailing beans to Bali's plantations and the famously unusual kopi luwak.
foods.whereToTry: Coffee plantations in Bali and Sumatra, and warungs nationwide.

practicalIntro: The essentials, current for 2026. Indonesia is generally straightforward to travel in, with its sheer size and occasional bureaucratic quirks the practicalities that most often catch visitors out.

practical.language: Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia) nationally, alongside hundreds of regional languages; English is widely spoken in tourist areas.
practical.money: Cash still matters outside big cities and malls, though card and e-wallet payments are increasingly common in Bali and Jakarta.
practical.visa: Visa-free or visa-on-arrival entry for up to 30 days for many nationalities including the US, Canada, Australia and UK, extendable once at an immigration office.
practical.plugs: Type C and F (Europlug/Schuko), 230 V, 50 Hz.
practical.emergency: 112 for general emergencies nationwide, or 110 (police) and 118/119 (ambulance).
practical.tipping: Not obligatory, but genuinely appreciated — rounding up or leaving 5-10% at restaurants without a service charge is common practice.
practical.safety: Generally safe for travellers, with petty theft and tourist-targeted scams the main everyday risks. Natural hazards — volcanoes, earthquakes and seasonal flooding — are a genuine, ongoing practical concern.
practical.connectivity: Excellent and cheap 4G in Bali, Java and other major islands; genuinely patchy in remote parts of eastern Indonesia including Raja Ampat.
practical.timeZone: Spans three zones — WIB (UTC+7) in Sumatra and Java including Jakarta, WITA (UTC+8) in Bali, Lombok and Komodo, and WIT (UTC+9) in Papua including Raja Ampat.

bestTime.headline: April–October for the dry season across most of the archipelago
bestTime.summary: Indonesia's equatorial climate genuinely means less seasonal temperature variation than many destinations, but the dry-versus-wet season split still shapes a trip significantly.

seasons.text: The genuinely most reliable window for hiking Bromo, diving Raja Ampat and touring Komodo, and also the busiest, most expensive season.
Genuinely good weather odds with noticeably thinner crowds than peak July–August.
Genuinely still workable for Bali and Java, with short, heavy daily downpours rather than constant rain, though rougher seas can disrupt boat trips.
Varies each year — some Java restaurants keep shorter daytime hours, though Bali and tourist areas are genuinely largely unaffected.

bestTime.avoid: Avoid booking boat-heavy Komodo or Raja Ampat trips deep in wet season (December–February), when rough seas most often disrupt island-hopping.

tripDuration.headline: 10–14 days for a first trip
tripDuration.summary: Indonesia's scale genuinely makes a single trip covering everything unrealistic — picking two or three regions well beats a rushed island-hopping itinerary.

options.text: Bali alone — Ubud, Seminyak or Kuta, and a day trip or two — the classic short Indonesia trip.
options.detail: Genuinely the most popular short itinerary, and complete enough on its own.

options.text: Bali plus Java — add Yogyakarta, Borobudur and Mount Bromo to a Bali base for real cultural and volcanic depth.
options.detail: The itinerary on this page, connecting Bali and Java by a short domestic flight.

options.text: Bali, Java and Komodo — add Labuan Bajo and Komodo National Park for dragons and island-hopping by boat.
options.detail: A genuinely complete first circuit of Indonesia's most famous sights.

options.text: Add Raja Ampat, Lombok's Gili Islands or Lake Toba, both genuinely worth dedicated time rather than a rushed detour.
options.detail: Raja Ampat and Lake Toba are where a second Indonesia trip belongs.

transport.intro: Domestic flights genuinely do most of the heavy lifting in Indonesia — this is an archipelago, and distances between regions are far too large to drive.

options.text: Genuinely essential for connecting [[ubud|Bali]], [[yogyakarta-borobudur|Java]], [[komodo-flores|Komodo]] and [[raja-ampat|Raja Ampat]].
options.detail: Budget carriers like Lion Air and Citilink connect most major airports affordably.

options.text: Genuinely the easiest way to get around cities and towns, with fixed upfront pricing and no haggling.
options.detail: Widely used in Bali, Java and other major islands; less available on smaller islands.

options.text: A genuinely common, affordable way to see [[ubud|Bali]] or [[yogyakarta-borobudur|Yogyakarta]] at your own pace with a local driver.
options.detail: Typically booked by the day through a hotel or driver directly.

options.text: The genuinely standard way to explore [[komodo-flores|Komodo National Park]] and [[raja-ampat|Raja Ampat]]'s scattered islands.
options.detail: Multi-day liveaboard boats are the classic way to see Komodo's islands properly.

options.text: A genuinely comfortable, scenic way to move between Java's cities, though the rail network doesn't extend to most other islands.
options.detail: Executive-class trains connect Jakarta, Bandung and Yogyakarta reliably.

culture.intro: Indonesian culture genuinely varies enormously by island and religion, but shares a strong nationwide emphasis on politeness, community and religious respect.

etiquette.title: Dress modestly at temples and mosques
etiquette.text: A sarong and sash are genuinely required at Balinese temples, usually available to rent or borrow at the entrance; cover shoulders and knees at mosques.

etiquette.title: Use your right hand
etiquette.text: Genuinely eat, pass items and shake hands with your right hand — the left is traditionally considered unclean.

etiquette.title: Keep your cool in disagreements
etiquette.text: Public displays of anger or raised voices are genuinely considered a loss of face — calm, indirect communication works far better.

etiquette.title: Remove shoes before entering homes and some temples
etiquette.text: A genuinely standard courtesy, and often enforced at temple entrances specifically.

etiquette.title: Respect prayer times and Ramadan
etiquette.text: In Muslim-majority areas, genuinely be mindful of call-to-prayer timings and, during Ramadan, of eating discreetly in public during fasting hours.

etiquette.title: Tipping is appreciated, not demanded
etiquette.text: Rounding up or leaving a small tip is genuinely a welcome gesture, though never strictly required.

dos: Dress modestly and wear a sarong when visiting temples.
Bargain politely and with good humour at markets — it's genuinely expected.
Carry small rupiah notes for warungs, temples and local transport.
Book domestic flights and Komodo or Raja Ampat trips well ahead in peak season.
donts: Don't touch anyone's head, including children's — it's considered genuinely disrespectful.
Don't point with your index finger — use your thumb or a whole open hand instead.
Don't underestimate travel times between islands — distances here are genuinely much larger than they look on a map.
Don't swim at Komodo or Raja Ampat sites without checking currents and tides first.

tipsIntro: The things that most often go wrong on an Indonesia trip, in rough order of how much they cost people.
tips: Book domestic flights and any Komodo or Raja Ampat liveaboard well ahead for dry-season travel.
Carry your passport or a copy — some island transfers and hotel check-ins genuinely require it.
Budget extra time for island transfers — ferries and flights are more weather-dependent than they first appear.
Bring reef-safe sunscreen, genuinely required at many marine parks including Raja Ampat.
Negotiate driver and tour prices upfront, genuinely before you get in the car or boat.
Stay hydrated and pace yourself in the heat, especially on temple visits and volcano treks.
Check current volcanic activity advisories before any Bromo or Ijen trek.
Keep small rupiah notes on hand — many warungs and local transport don't take cards.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Indonesia?
faq.a: Ten to fourteen days covers Bali and Java comfortably, which is the itinerary on this page. Five to seven days is enough for Bali alone, and genuinely still worthwhile.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit Indonesia?
faq.a: April to October, the dry season, for the most reliable weather across Bali, Java, Komodo and beyond; the wet season still works for Bali specifically, with shorter daily downpours.

faq.q: Do you need to fly between Indonesian islands?
faq.a: For anywhere beyond a single island, genuinely yes — domestic flights or ferries are the standard way to connect Bali, Java, Komodo and further afield.
No, genuinely one of Southeast Asia's better-value destinations — mid-range travel runs about Rp 800,000–1,600,000 per person per day, with domestic flights and dive trips the main added cost.

faq.q: Can you see Komodo dragons in the wild?
faq.a: Yes, genuinely, on Komodo and Rinca islands within Komodo National Park, on a short guided walk with a ranger — no zoo required.

Generally yes, genuinely safe for travellers, with petty theft and scams the main everyday risk. Natural hazards — volcanic activity and earthquakes — are a real, ongoing consideration worth checking before remote trips.
